name: Coding Help That Teaches
title: Coding Help That Teaches
answer: Coding help that teaches means using AI in computer science classes to explain errors and prompt student thinking rather than to produce corrected code. It matters because AI can write working code in seconds, so a student can finish an assignment without learning anything. The book's principle is that a coding tool should explain what an error message means and ask the student what they think is wrong, not write the fix.

sections.body: Computer science faces a particular problem with AI because tools can write working code almost instantly. A student who is stuck on an error can ask for the fix, paste it in, watch the program run, and turn in the assignment while learning nothing. Coding help that teaches solves this by changing what the tool does: it explains the meaning of an error message and asks the student what they believe is wrong, instead of supplying the corrected code. The book says tools used in schools should be set up this way wherever possible. The aim is to keep the student doing the thinking that the assignment was meant to produce.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a classroom, the tool's role is to interpret error messages and ask the student what they think is wrong, leaving the actual correction to the student. The book gives age rules for access. GitHub Copilot, a popular coding assistant, is available through its education program only to verified students aged 13 and older. Code.org is designed for all ages, and students under 13 use accounts set up by a teacher or school. For younger students, the teacher can demonstrate coding help on a shared screen rather than giving students direct access.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels the research on this as sobering. In a university programming course, students were split into three groups: one used a tutor that gave hints, one used a chatbot that could give full solutions, and one used no AI. Both AI groups scored higher on the exercise, but neither learned more than the group without AI (Bassner et al., 2026), and the students preferred the chatbot that helped them least. A review of generative AI in computer science education also flagged the risk of AI errors and invented information in code help (Adejumo et al., 2026). The book notes that those studies involved university students and that similar research in schools has not yet been found, though the principle still points in a clear direction for schools.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The book sets several limits. AI help in code carries the risk of errors and invented information, as flagged in the review it cites. The evidence comes from university students, and similar research in schools has not yet been found, so the direction is a principle rather than a proven school result. Age rules decide who gets direct access: GitHub Copilot through its education program is only for verified students 13 and older, and Code.org is designed for all ages with students under 13 using accounts set up by a teacher or school. For younger students, the teacher can demonstrate coding help on a shared screen rather than giving students direct access, which keeps the decision about tool use with the teacher.
